cards.title: CAC-to-LTV and Payback Thresholds for Aggressive Scaling
cards.summary: IM8's scaling gate: 3.0-3.5x CAC:LTV on a 24-month horizon with blended payback under 4 months.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether your store's unit economics can support a spend increase, or setting the internal threshold before raising daily ad budget.
steps: Compute LTV on an explicit 24-month horizon rather than a 12-month or first-order basis, so repeat purchases and subscription renewals are included. IM8 targets a CAC-to-LTV ratio of 3.0-3.5x on that 24-month window.
Track payback period on a blended basis (across all products and channels), not per-SKU. IM8 runs under 4 months blended, which is what allows very high daily spend without cash strain.

Before scaling spend, test whether your current payback still clears your threshold after the planned increase; if ad costs rise with budget, payback lengthens even if CAC:LTV looks acceptable on trailing data.
Treat 3.0-3.5x and under-4-months as IM8's source-specific heuristics, not universal benchmarks. Your acceptable ratio depends on gross margin, refund rate, and how much working capital you can hold.

Use the ratio as a gate on new SKUs: IM8 runs three core SKUs (Daily Ultimate Essentials, Longevity, Beckham stack), so a new product must justify its own payback math before getting significant spend.
caveats: The 3.0-3.5x and <4 month figures are IM8's targets at $150K-$300K/day spend, not proven minimums for smaller stores.
Blended payback can mask a poorly performing SKU or channel; check contribution-level payback before assuming the blend protects you.
cards.source_name: How He Hit $100M in Under a Year (And Why You Won't).docx

cards.title: Platform Mix for Scaling: 85/15 Meta to Google
cards.summary: IM8 allocates 85% of spend to Meta and 15% to Google while exploring podcasts, YouTube, AppLovin, TikTok and CTV.
cards.use_when: Setting or defending your paid acquisition channel allocation when planning a budget increase.
steps: Anchor the bulk of paid budget in the platform with the deepest creative testing surface. IM8 runs roughly 85% Meta and 15% Google while spending $150K-$300K/day, treating Meta as the primary scaling engine.
Keep Google funded as a demand-capture layer rather than a discovery channel; a minority share is enough to harvest search intent the Meta mix generates.

Earmark a small exploration budget for adjacent channels (IM8 was evaluating podcasts, YouTube, AppLovin, TikTok and CTV). Do not redistribute core budget to them until they show payback on the same CAC:LTV and payback standard as the core mix.
Because creative volume is the constraint on Meta scale, treat any new channel as a creative-format project too (podcast reads, CTV spots), not just a line-item budget move.
Review allocation when either platform's marginal cost rises; a fixed 85/15 split is a starting posture, not a rule.
Verify current platform capabilities and attribution behavior before committing budget, since ad platform interfaces and measurement change often.
caveats: This mix reflects a large-spend supplements brand; smaller budgets may not reach statistical significance across five-plus channels.
Exploration channels were being evaluated, not proven at scale, in this source.
cards.source_name: How He Hit $100M in Under a Year (And Why You Won't).docx

cards.title: Running 1,500 Concurrent Ads with a Daily Feedback Loop
cards.summary: High creative volume plus daily iteration is the operating system behind IM8's paid social scale.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing your ad creative production pipeline when paid social performance has plateaued.
steps: Treat volume as infrastructure: IM8 runs around 1,500 active ads simultaneously. Plan production output around the number of concepts and variants you can sustain weekly, not one-off campaign launches.
Build a deep daily feedback loop: review performance early, kill losers, and push spend to winners within the same day so learnings feed the next batch of creative.
Organize the pipeline so statics and video share one testing queue; format is a variable inside the same testing system, not a separate calendar.
Separate concept generation from production. IM8 uses AI for static generation to compress the production step while humans still define the angles and claims.
Track which concepts survive across weeks, not just which single ad wins today; the durable output is reusable winning angles, not individual ads.
Confirm current ad-account limits and review tooling for your platform, as policies and interfaces change.
caveats: Sustaining 1,500 active ads requires production capacity and spend volume; at low budgets a large active count can fragment learning.
Daily iteration only works with fast, trustworthy reporting; lagging attribution undercuts the loop.
cards.source_name: How He Hit $100M in Under a Year (And Why You Won't).docx

cards.title: Shifting Production to AI-Generated Statics (75/25 Mix)
cards.summary: IM8 moved to 75% statics and 25% video, using AI for static generation, and reports 200M views from AI-generated video.
cards.use_when: Rebalancing your creative format mix to increase output speed and lower production cost.
steps: Reassess the assumed primacy of video. IM8 shifted so statics are about 75% of production and video about 25%, citing speed of iteration as the driver.
Use AI static generation where the constraint is how fast you can produce variations of a proven angle; this lets you test many executions of the same concept cheaply.
Keep video for angles that genuinely need motion (demonstrations, founder story, athlete content), rather than defaulting every concept to video.
Track performance by format within the same campaign structure so you can see whether statics hold up at your spend level; IM8's shift is a result of their own testing, not a universal finding.
Test AI-generated video as a distinct bet: IM8 reports 200M views on AI-generated video, but treat virality as an upside, not the basis of your acquisition plan.
Re-verify platform policies on AI-generated ad content, which change over time.
caveats: The 75/25 static-to-video ratio is IM8's current split, not a recommended default for every category or audience.
View counts are not conversions; validate AI creative against your own CPA and payback metrics.

cards.title: 3-Month Upfront Subscription to Lift AOV and Cash Flow
cards.summary: Pricing a 90-day upfront subscription at $235 versus $89/month raises IM8's global AOV to $280 and improves logistics.
cards.use_when: Designing or restructuring subscription plans, prepaid bundles, or billing cadence on a consumable product.
steps: Offer a prepaid multi-month tier alongside monthly billing. IM8 prices a 3-month subscription at $235 upfront versus $89 per month, giving customers a clear discount for committing.
Track the AOV effect of the upfront tier. IM8 reports the structure lifting AOV to $280 globally, because prepaid buyers add more than a single month's order.
Account for the logistics benefit: fewer shipments per customer over the same period lowers fulfillment and shipping cost, which is part of why the upfront structure is attractive beyond cash.
Position the upfront plan as the default or hero option on the offer page, with monthly billing as the alternative, so the prepaid commitment is the path of least resistance.
Set the discount depth with margin math: the gap between $235 and three months at $89 (about $267) is the effective incentive; adjust to your own contribution margin.
For consumer protection and refund policy, confirm what happens on cancellation of a prepaid plan in your jurisdiction before launching.
caveats: The $235, $89/month and $280 AOV figures are IM8-specific; your price points and AOV lift will differ.
Prepaid plans shift refund and churn exposure earlier; make sure cancellation terms are clear to avoid chargebacks.
cards.source_name: How He Hit $100M in Under a Year (And Why You Won't).docx

cards.title: Recognizing Revenue Upfront with Quarterly Billing
cards.summary: IM8's quarterly upfront billing lets a public company recognize subscription revenue immediately rather than over the term.
cards.use_when: Deciding subscription billing cadence when accounting treatment, cash timing or investor reporting matters to your store.
steps: If upfront billing is acceptable to your customers, collecting for a full quarter at purchase changes when cash arrives and, for IM8, allows revenue recognition up front. This matters most when you report to public markets or investors.
Weigh the accounting and finance benefit against conversion: an upfront charge raises the commitment barrier, so pair it with a clear discount and value stack (as IM8 does with its 3-month tier).

Coordinate with your accountant before assuming upfront recognition; rules depend on jurisdiction, your entity type, and contract terms (including refund rights), and the source is describing one company's approach.
Use the cash-timing advantage deliberately: earlier cash can fund ad spend or working capital, but only if payback math still holds.
Document cancellation and refund terms carefully, since they can affect both recognition and customer disputes.
caveats: Revenue recognition rules vary by accounting standard and jurisdiction; IM8's treatment is not a template for every seller.
Charging upfront can reduce trial conversion for price-sensitive audiences.

cards.title: Post-Purchase Value Stack: Masterclasses and VIP Access
cards.summary: IM8 retains 90-day subscribers by adding digital access to medical board masterclasses and celebrity trainer sessions.
cards.use_when: Improving retention or justifying a premium subscription tier by adding non-physical perks.
steps: Attach digital access to the prepaid tier rather than discounting further. IM8 adds quarterly masterclasses with its medical board and David Beckham's trainer to the 3-month subscription.
Choose perks that reinforce the product's credibility: expert-led content supports a supplements brand's health claims in a way generic rewards do not.
Use physical or experiential rewards sparingly as top-tier incentives. IM8 runs 'golden ticket' trips to Dubai to meet Sabalenka, which functions as a lottery-style acquisition and retention hook.
Build the perks into the subscription renewal pitch, so members see the next quarter's access as a reason to stay rather than a one-time bonus.
Track renewal and churn by tier to confirm the value stack pays for itself; the perks carry real cost in talent and production.
Confirm talent usage rights for content and trips, since these are contract-bound and time-limited.
caveats: Access to celebrity trainers and medical boards requires partnerships most brands do not have; substitute credible experts in your own niche.
Experiential perks like trips have high per-winner cost and should be treated as marketing spend with its own ROI analysis.
cards.source_name: How He Hit $100M in Under a Year (And Why You Won't).docx

cards.title: Long-Term Equity Partnerships with Tier-1 Athletes
cards.summary: IM8 structures minimum 3-year equity deals with David Beckham and Sabalenka instead of transactional influencer payments.
cards.use_when: Negotiating a major creator or celebrity partnership and choosing between flat fees and equity or long-term alignment.
steps: Structure partnerships as equity or long-term deals rather than one-off sponsored posts. IM8 has David Beckham as an equity partner, and Sabalenka on equity with a minimum 3-year term.
Buy alignment with duration: multi-year minimums mean the partner's payoff depends on the brand's growth, which sustains promotion beyond the launch window.
Give the partner operational involvement where credible. Beckham participates in weekly calls and taste-profile decisions, embedding him in product rather than only in ads.
Look for partners who are genuine power users of the product category (IM8 cites Sabalenka as a power user), because authentic usage supports the creative and reduces claim risk.
Diversify across several aligned athletes (IM8 also works with F1 driver Ollie Bearman and Giannis) rather than betting the brand on a single face.
Model the dilution and commitment before signing: equity is permanent cost, and 3-year minimums reduce flexibility if the partnership underperforms.
Get legal review of endorsement, equity and morality clauses; terms are jurisdiction- and deal-specific.
caveats: Tier-1 equity partnerships are only available to brands with traction and negotiating leverage; early-stage stores rarely have this option.
Equity deals carry long-term dilution risk and are hard to unwind if the partner's public profile changes.
cards.source_name: How He Hit $100M in Under a Year (And Why You Won't).docx

cards.title: Golden Ticket Experiences as a Wild-Bet Acquisition Hook
cards.summary: IM8 runs VIP giveaway experiences, such as trips to Dubai to meet Sabalenka, as high-attention acquisition and retention plays.
cards.use_when: Planning a promotional event or giveaway that needs to cut through paid social and drive both new customers and retention.
steps: Design the prize around access to the celebrity partner, not just product. IM8's golden ticket trips to Dubai to meet Sabalenka turn a giveaway into a story the partner's audience will share.
Tie entry to purchase or subscription so the mechanic drives orders rather than only list growth; this also keeps the promotion measurable against CAC.
Coordinate the giveaway with the partner's own channels so the reach compounds beyond your ad account.
Treat the experience as a 'wild bet' in your budget: IM8 frames these as non-transactional plays whose value is attention and brand association, not immediate tracked ROI.
Plan legal compliance for sweepstakes and travel prizes, including eligibility, taxes and disclosure, before promoting.
Measure halo effects (brand search, direct traffic, new-subscriber mix) alongside attributed conversions, since the mechanic's payoff is partly untracked.
caveats: Experiential prizes carry significant cost and compliance burden; small stores may not get proportional reach.
The source describes these as wild bets, meaning outcomes are uncertain and not guaranteed to pay back directly.
cards.source_name: How He Hit $100M in Under a Year (And Why You Won't).docx

cards.title: Choosing DTC Over Retail to Protect Focus
cards.summary: IM8 runs 100% DTC (98% site, 2% Amazon), ships to 31 countries, and declines major retail offers to stay focused for three years.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a retail distribution offer or deciding whether to keep selling exclusively through your own store.
steps: Calculate what retail distribution would do to your unit economics before accepting: retail margins, slotting, and slower cash cycles can undercut the payback math that funds your ad spend.
Recognize that DTC gives you direct control of creative, offer structure and first-party data, which is what makes a high-volume paid social model like IM8's possible.
Keep a small marketplace presence only where it is strategically useful; IM8 runs about 2% on Amazon while keeping 98% on its own site.
If you decline retail, set a time horizon for the decision (IM8 frames it as the next three years) so the choice is a strategy rather than drift.
When expanding internationally, prioritize markets your existing DTC infrastructure can serve; IM8 ships to 31 countries without a retail intermediary.
Re-evaluate if customer acquisition costs rise faster than your DTC margin can absorb; the DTC-only stance is a trade-off, not a universal rule.
caveats: DTC-only limits reach in markets where retail discovery drives most category purchase.
Declining retail offers forgoes revenue and distribution that may be hard to renegotiate later.

cards.title: Holding Bitcoin on the Balance Sheet
cards.summary: IM8's parent deploys excess corporate cash into Bitcoin, an example of treasury policy tied to a founder's conviction rather than an operating necessity.
cards.use_when: Considering what to do with surplus cash as a brand, or interpreting founder-led treasury decisions at a company you compete with or invest in.
steps: Separate operating decisions from treasury decisions: IM8's Bitcoin position is a balance-sheet choice made alongside, not instead of, funding ad spend and payback-positive growth.
If you consider a volatile treasury asset, size it so a large drawdown would not impair ad budget, inventory purchasing or payroll.
Recognize this is a founder-conviction play with real volatility and accounting complexity; it is not a growth tactic and has no direct effect on CAC, AOV or retention.
For public or investor-facing entities, confirm accounting and disclosure treatment with counsel and auditors before taking such a position.
caveats: Bitcoin is volatile and may be inappropriate as a treasury asset for most ecommerce operators.
The source presents this as one founder's choice, not a recommended financial practice.
